p: Permission granted.

First, I want to give a huge thank you to Council Member De La Rosa and Speaker Menin on the paraprofessional bills. And, OG Council Member Keith Powers, we still remember you even though you're up there. I also want to give a huge thank you to my community for starting, organizing, and petitioning to landmark Saint Mary's Church on Grand Street. So I want to give a huge thank you to Norma Ramirez, Sandra Stuthers, who's the TA president at Grand Street Guild, Ray Klein, who also helped with the petitioning, and of course Lower East Side

Preservation Initiative, who did the landmarking application pro bono for the residents of the Lower East Side, as well as the Archdiocese for receiving this ask from the community and being supportive of the application, thank you all. I vote aye.
Thank you. Council Member Mealy?
(ABSENT)
Council Member Morano?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

I wanted to speak a moment on Intro 692. I'll be voting yes enthusiastically on this legislation. I want to congratulate Council Member Carmen De La Rosa for getting this bill across the finish line. I also want to recognize former Council Member Keith Powers, whose leadership on this issue helped lay the groundwork for where we are today. I don't know that anybody told him he's a former council member,

though, because I feel like I see him at City Hall just as much now as when he served in this body. He's kind of like the municipal equivalent of Bruce Willis in The Sixth Sense, but it's great to see him. Every day, our school paraprofessionals do some of the hardest and most important work in our education system. They help children with disabilities learn, communicate, and succeed. They support our teachers, strengthen classrooms, and make a real difference in the lives of New York families. Yet for far too long, they've been asked to do that work for far too little pay. I do have one regret in this bill, though. A wonderful paraprofessional from my district, Ellen Santorelli (phonetic), devoted her career to serving our children. She retired yesterday, and because of the timing, she won't receive this benefit. That's unfortunate because people like Ellen are exactly the public servants struggling to afford to continue to live here that we should be rewarding. I also wish this $10,000 payment could be pensionable. Unfortunately, this legislation doesn't

permit that. My hope is that making compensation like this pensionable becomes part of the next collective bargaining agreement so these hardworking employees receive not only immediate relief but greater retirement security as well. Finally, I think it's disappointing that this administration has indicated its opposition to this and other similar legislation. Too often, when it comes to giving working people the support they've earned, whether it's paraprofessionals, EMS workers, or others, we're told that collective bargaining means nothing can be done. Collective bargaining is obviously important, and it must be respected, but it shouldn't become an excuse (TIMER) for not helping working folks in our city. Thank you. With that, I'll vote aye on everything with the exception of Intro 972 and 983-A, on which I vote no.
Thank you. Council Member Narcisse?

I want to disclose that my son works for a nonprofit that is

being funded by us, and my hubby is a medical doctor at NYU. And permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Thank you, Majority. I am proud to support Intro 692. First, I have to say thank you to Carmen and, of course, Keith and our Chair. Today, we were able to pass it through, and I want to say thank you to all the leadership who have been advocating for the paraprofessionals, and congratulations to all of you. Amazing. You've been doing the work, and the city that's supposed to be the leading city, and we were not being present for you. So today we're saying that we are with you, we are for you, we are supporting you. I'm proud to support it, the Respect Check for our paraprofessionals. I have sat down with you in my office. I have seen firsthand that you do the work in the classroom. I used to be the mom in the classroom, and

I've seen you guys, really, you work. You are working for the most vulnerable kids, and we are talking about our future. So now, with our future, we are saying that the starting salary is just not sustainable in the city of New York. We ask them, the paraprofessionals, to do some of the most demanding work in our schools, and we have not let them, you know, we never let them know that we care for them in their paycheck. We let them go further, deeper into poverty, I will say. We made a mistake, but this bill is not just a substitute for the raise. They deserve it, and they had bargained for it, so now let's continue to make sure they get what they deserve in New York City. With nearly 1,600 para vacancies citywide, we cannot afford to keep losing our professionals. They are very special to us, and let's show it. Let's continue making sure that they get what they deserve in New York City. And on that note, I vote aye on all. (TIMER)

Perfect, thank you.

Council Member Nurse?
I vote aye. Congratulations, Council Member De La Rosa.
I just want to remind everyone to stay here, so we can keep the numbers that we need in the room. Thank you.
Council Member Ossé? COUNCIL MEMBER OSSÉ: I vote aye. Congratulations, Council Member De La Rosa.
Council Member Paladino?
(ABSENT)
Council Member Restler?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Thank you so much, Majority Leader. I, as the Speaker mentioned, would have strongly preferred for us to be resolving compensation for paraprofessionals through the collective bargaining process. But it has become unfortunately apparent over many years that pattern

bargaining is failing the lowest paid workers in city government. There are too many workers, like paraprofessionals, who earn $32,500 a year, where a 3% raise just doesn't mean much. If you're well compensated and you're making over $100,000 a year, a 3% raise is great. But the nature of pattern bargaining really expands upon and exacerbates the inequities that exist in compensation in New York City. And so we need OLR and the Mamdani Administration to begin creating equity tables where each year they identify low-wage workers in city government who are underpaid and prioritize bringing those wages up. But until that happens, we can't afford not to act. And so I'm grateful for the leadership of our former Labor Chair, Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, for ensuring that these paraprofessionals get the support that they deserve, and I appreciate Speaker Menin's leadership and the Council today, along with the UFT, in delivering for low-wage workers who deserve this and so much more.

I'm grateful to every paraprofessional in New York City for their hard work in taking care of our kids. I proudly vote aye on all.
Council Member Riley?
I just want to state for the record that my children are scholars at New York City Public Schools, and we are also members of the YMCA. And I vote aye on all.
Thank you. Council Member Salaam?
I just want to say for the record that my family are members of the YMCA. And I am proud to vote aye on all.
Council Member Justin Sanchez?
I’d like to disclose I have nothing to disclose. Aye on all. (LAUGHTER)
Thank you. Council Member Pierina Sanchez?

I’d like to disclose on the record that my sibling works at CUNY.

And permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Thank you, Majority Leader. I want to say congratulations to Council Member De La Rosa and the Speaker for your leadership on Intro 692. Thirty-two thousand dollars is not enough. Our paras deserve more. And I want to agree with Council Member Ariola that our EMTs absolutely do too. In my district, the way that the shortfall of our EMTs shows up is that NYPD patrol cars are taking people to hospitals every single day instead of EMTs. So I hear the uproar, and I agree. And I also remind my colleagues that there are so many New York cities within our city. In my district, the median income is $25,000 a year for a worker. And so $32,000 is not enough for our paras. And, $25,000 a year is not enough for folks in my district. So let's please continue to fight our inequalities, expand opportunity, and tax the rich so we can fund the key initiatives that can get us there. Thank you.
Council Member Sanchez?
Aye on all.
Thank you. Council Member Santosuosso?
Aye on all.
Thank you. Council Member Schulman?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Paraprofessionals are the backbone of our classrooms, supporting students with special needs, assisting teachers, and keeping our schools safe and inclusive. Yet for too long, their pay has not reflected the essential role they play. Intro 692-A is about respect, equity, and justice, and correcting the wage disparities created by years of pattern bargaining that have left paraprofessionals behind. This bill recognizes the value of your work and sends a clear message: New York City cannot deliver quality education without

investing in the people who make it possible. I want to congratulate Carmen De La Rosa and Speaker Menin. And by the way, this isn't the first piece of important legislation that has had new life in this session. I am a proud co-sponsor of this legislation. I was also the last go-round. And with that, I vote aye on all.
Council Member Stevens?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

One, I would like to be associated with the remarks of Council Member Sanchez, and also would like to uplift at the same time the position of EMS and us having very low wages in our district. My average being at $36,000 a year. I also would like to highlight nonprofit workers. I mean, today, hearing everyone just speak about how it is a disgrace that paraprofessionals are being paid $32,000, I would love and hope that the same energy continues for nonprofit workers who work tirelessly in jobs that are honestly thankless. And

although I know Epstein said he was making more at a nonprofit, that is typically not the case, where most nonprofit workers' average income is about $40,000, who are doing all the work that we all glorify and uplift here. So, I just want to continue to say a shoutout to Council Member De La Rosa for getting us across the field, but also just making sure that we as a council continue to prioritize all workers who are struggling at the bottom and who are making very low wages compared to all other New Yorkers. We need to be thinking about how we continue to push forward legislation and support for those who are in the most need in all these communities. Thank you.
Apologies, Council Member Stevens... (CROSS-TALK)
Aye on all.
Thank you, Council Member Stevens. Council Member Thomas-Henry?

I'd like to disclose that my daughter is a participant at Jamaica

Center for Arts and Learning. And I’d like permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

I'd like to acknowledge a constituent, someone who has known me— whoo! — probably since I was three years old, and has always been a close family friend and a community auntie who is a para and who actually introduced me to this bill as an advocate even before I was elected. So I want to say we're bringing it home. Thank you, Miss Gina Lewis (phonetic). Thank you to my colleague Council Member De La Rosa for carrying this bill, and to Speaker Menin. I vote aye on all.
Council Member Ung?
Aye on all.
Council Member Vernikov?
Thank you, Majority Leader. I move for unanimous consent to vote on all Land Use Call-ups as well as coupled General Orders.
Seeing no objections.
Thank you. Aye on all, with the exception of Intro 972 and 983-A, for which I vote no. Thank you.
Council Member Williams?
I am disclosing on the record that I am affiliated with CUNY. And I would like permission to explain my vote.
Permission granted.

Thank you so much, Majority Leader. One of the greatest responsibilities we have as legislators is to build public trust. Sometimes that means creating transparent processes for the decisions government makes. Other times, it means taking an honest look at the history that has shaped our city. Today we're doing both. Legislation implementing the recommendations of the Quadrennial Advisory Commission, which we thank, reflects this Council's commitment to a transparent, independent, and

predictable process for reviewing elected officials' compensation. Government is strongest when New Yorkers understand not only the decisions we make but the process behind them. We're also taking an important step toward acknowledging one of the darkest chapters in New York City's history. The Draft Riots of 1863, which included horrific acts of racial violence against Black New Yorkers, yet there remains no formal public acknowledgement of those events in our city's landscape. I want to thank my constituent, Nia Clark, whose reporting on Cheryl Wills, NY1, helped bring renewed attention to the Draft Riots. I want to thank Speaker Julie Menin for her leadership, council staff, committee members, and chairs for their work on these measures and all of my colleagues for their partnership. And very briefly, in my 53 seconds, as I was just sharing with the Speaker that I have a staffer, my special assistant Kate, who started working for me... No, this is now-- I can do this now...
It's during General Discussion.
No, this is not my interns. This is about the para bill.
My apologies. Y'all can all laugh at me now.
Can I have my 10 seconds back, Majority Leader?
Yeah, please give her seconds back. That's my apologies (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)

You're the best. Very quickly, Kate, my special assistant, started working for me. She's a constituent part-time. When I first got into the Council, she eventually moved to fulltime. She was a para, and one of the things that she mentioned was the salary, and I was able to give her a higher salary. And perhaps, if her salary were higher, sadly, I might not have her in our office. I'm thankful, but I'm just really excited for this bill and for people like Kate. Thank you so much, Majority Leader. And congrats, Chair De La Rosa.
Thank you. Council Member Wilson?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Thank you, Majority Leader. I'm proud that District 3 is a beacon for dreamers and strivers from around the nation and the world, to young actors aspiring to make it on Broadway, to queer people yearning for a chosen family, and to visitors taking in the neon lights of Times Square. And that's long been the case in District 3. Take the Lithuanian Alliance Building in Chelsea, whose landmark designation I am proud to support today. From the late 19th through 20th centuries, after making it through Ellis Island, the first port of call for newly arrived Lithuanian Americans was 307 West 30th Street. There they'd get a friendly welcome, assistance with housing and employment, and

maybe a copy of the Tevyne (phonetic) newspaper printed on site. The Lithuanian Alliance Building inspires us to extend a hand to newcomers with warmth, hospitality, and professionalism. It also represents the ever-important bonds of friendship, draugystė, between Lithuania and the United States. I'd like to acknowledge the Consul General of Lithuania, as well as the staff members and board members of the Alliance Building. And I'd like to thank my colleagues for joining me in supporting the landmark designation for the Lithuanian Alliance Center. Sveskimė kartū (phonetic). And I vote aye on all.
Thank you. Council Member Won?
I just want to publicly disclose that one of my children is part of the public school system. And I vote aye on all.
Council Member Wong?
Permission to explain my vote?
Permission granted.

Thank you, Majority Leader. In my district, there are just so, so many constituents who are living paycheck to paycheck and having problems making ends meet. And with that in mind-- and also I spent many months advocating for savings into the city budget, of identifying savings. So I cannot consciously vote on a bill to increase a salary for myself. So, I vote aye on all, except for Intro 983-A. And I also vote no on 972 on the tax credit decrease, which would actually increase city taxes. Thank you.
Council Member Zhuang?
For the record, my kids go to public school, which we are funding in New York City. I also want permission to explain my vote.
Permission granted.

First of all, I want to say congratulations to paras. I also want to congratulate our small business owners because today,

we are voting on a bill, Intro 955-A, the Red Tape Relief Act. That's a big win for our small business owners because, first of all, they are the backbone of New York City's economy. They create jobs, strengthen our neighborhood, and they represent the dream of hard-working families. But too many regulations, too many permits, they have to get before they get that door open, even make a penny, before they make a penny. So this bill, Intro 955-A, offers a practical solution. It requires city agencies to coordinate inspections and the plan review instead of making business owners navigate to one agency after another. We know this approach works because New York City has done it before through the New Business Acceleration Team, which helps a business open faster by improving coordination across agencies. Intro 955-A also ensures accountability. This legislation requires public reporting so we can measure whether this program is actually reducing the delay and helping business success.

And also, I want to thank our Speaker and a lot of colleagues who helped me work on this bill and supported this bill. Our job is to make sure the government is more efficient and also to make our small business owners' lives easier. So I want to thank everyone who voted yes on this bill, and I will vote yes on the bill. I vote aye on all (TIMER) except Intro 983-A, which is a no.
Thank you, Council Member. Council Member Carr?
I would like to second the comments of colleagues in support of our EMTs. And I vote aye on all, with the exception of Introductions 972 and 983-A, on which I vote no.
Council Member Abreu?
Aye.
Speaker Menin?
I vote aye on all, except Preconsidered Intro 983-A, on which I abstain. (PAUSE)

All items on today’s General Order Calendar have been adopted by a

vote of 49 in the affirmative, 0 in the negative, and no abstentions, with the exception of Intro 972-A, which was adopted by a vote of 43 in the affirmative, 6 in the negative, and 0 abstentions, and Intro 983-A, which was adopted by a vote of 43 in the affirmative, 6 in the negative and 0 abstentions (sic), and Intro 913-A, which was adopted by a vote of 48 in the affirmative, 1 in the negative, and 0 abstentions. The revised Land Use Call-ups vote is 48 in the affirmative and 0 in the negative. Congratulations. (APPLAUSE)
Just give me one second. Intro 983-A was adopted by a vote of 43 in the affirmative, 5 in the negative, and 1 abstention. Congrats again. Introduction and Reading of bills?
All bills have been referred to Committee as indicated on today’s agenda.

Thank you. We will now move into the Discussion of Resolutions. We have

two folks signed up, Council Member Salaam, followed by Council Member Louis.

Thank you, Majority Leader Abreu. Colleagues, I want to take a moment before we vote on Resolution 371, because this one deserves more than just a procedural eye. First, I want to thank Council Members Farías, Louis, Narcisse, and Wilson for supporting this resolution. And thank you to Deputy Speaker Williams for holding the vote in the committee. Fatman Scoop, known as Isaac Freeman III, was born right here in Manhattan on August 6th, 1968. Harlem raised him, Cardinal Hayes shaped him, and then he went out and gave this city and this world something they will never forget. That voice, that energy, that call and response that turned every room he walked into a celebration. For a decade, he held down midnight to 5:00 A.M. slots on Hot 97. He collaborated with some of the greatest artists of our generation. He won a Grammy, crossed genres, crossed continents, and everywhere he went, people felt it.

But I want my colleagues to know something beyond the accolades. He was my friend. (TIMER) Well, that was quick. (LAUGHS)
I'll give you an extra 15 seconds, Council Member.
Oh, thank you.
And I'm going to be consistent with everybody else today. As you notice, I'm giving everybody an extra 10 seconds.

When I was inaugurated, he came and pulled up. He didn't have to do that. Nobody asked him to do it. But that was Isaac. He showed up for the people he loved the same way that he showed up for every audience with everything he had, every single time. We lost him on August 30th of 2024, at 56 years of age, on stage, doing exactly what he was born to do. This resolution asks that every August 6th, the City...
Council Member, you have to wrap up.

Yes, sir... the City of New York pauses and remembers him, not just as an artist, a son of Harlem, as someone who made this city feel like home for everyone who heard his voice. Thank you. I ask my colleagues to vote yes on Resolution 371. Thank you.
Council Member Louis?

Thank you, Mr. Majority Leader. I would like to thank Council Member Salaam for sponsoring Resolution 371 and for giving us the opportunity to honor a man who meant so much to so many. For most people, Fatman Scoop was the voice, the booming, raw, unmistakable energy that could fill any room, any club, any track he touched. He was the ultimate hip-hop hype man, and he did it with joy every single time. But for me, Fatman Scoop was something more personal. He was my boss. I had the privilege of working for him at Hot 97, pulling his press clips every morning, breaking news stories,

and making sure he had everything he needed to walk into that studio ready. And he was always ready. What I didn't expect was how much he would pour into me. He saw my ambition to be a journalist and to work in media, and he didn't just encourage me; he pushed me. He told me to keep fighting for where I needed to be. He showed me how to use the equipment. (TIMER) Wow, that was fast. (LAUGHS) With all that said, I'm proud to vote in support of this resolution designating August 6th as Fatman Scoop Recognition Day in the City of New York. Thank you.

Seeing no one else signed up to speak on Resolutions, we will now have a voice vote on today’s Resos. If you wish to vote against or abstain from today's Resolution, please notify the Legislative Documents Unit by email or by approaching the dais. I will now read today’s resolution into the record. Resolution 371 declares August 6th annually as Fatman Scoop Recognition Day in the City

of New York, and celebrates the signature style that he brought to every musical collaboration and the inimitable energy he brought to every audience. Will all those in favor say aye?
Aye
All opposed say nay?
(SILENT)
Any abstentions?
(SILENT)

The ayes have it. And I would also like to provide a revision of the vote on Intro 983-A, which was adopted by a vote of 42 in the affirmative, 6 in the negative, and 1 abstention. We will now move into General Discussion, beginning with Deputy Speaker Williams, followed by Council Member Louis.

Thank you so much, Majority Leader. Following the rules, I just want to give a special shoutout to my D27 summer interns: Avani,

Ryan, Maribel, Eric, and Owen, who are joining us in the Chambers today. Thank you so much for your hard work, your curiosity, and your commitment to public service. I am so grateful to have you with us this summer. Thank you.
Congratulations, interns. Council Member Louis, followed by Council Member Wong.

Thank you. Today I'm introducing Intro 978, a bill that will increase the qualifying income limit for seniors and persons with disabilities for the senior citizen rent increase exemption-- SCRIE and DRIE. This bill is imperative to protect our most vulnerable populations from increasing housing costs and prevent displacement. New York City faces a severe housing crisis, which is exacerbated by rent increases that threaten housing stability for New Yorkers. Our seniors and neighbors with disabilities rely heavily on SCRIE and DRIE because many live on fixed incomes. These programs allow our older adults

to afford their daily essentials without having to choose between buying groceries, purchasing medicine, and paying for rent. As of June 2026, New York City experienced another unprecedented housing price increase, with the median monthly rent being $5,295 in Manhattan compared to $4,350 in Brooklyn. These escalating rent costs reflect a widening disparity of housing affordability across the city. We must protect our low-income residents from being priced out of neighborhoods they have called home for decades. This bill addresses the eligibility challenges we face as New Yorkers, strengthening housing security for tenants, ultimately lowering tenant turnover for landlords, and reducing eviction risk for tenants. Homelessness is already a widespread issue in New York City, and fewer affordable units will only increase shelter populations. A recent report showed that 26,000 applications were received for just 84 affordable senior housing units in the city. It is important that we continue to protect our older

adults and uniquely abled New Yorkers from experiencing traumatic displacement. I urge my colleagues to support Intro 978. Thank you.
Council Member Wong, followed by Santosuosso.

Thank you, Majority Leader. Today, I'm introducing Intro 984, legislation to formally establish a permanent citywide NYPD Street Takeover Unit. This bill was prompted by the dangerous April 18th takeover at 69th Street and Elliott Avenue in my district, where nearly 100 vehicles blocked the intersection, drivers performed stunts around a fire in the roadway between two gas stations, and individuals damaged a mock police vehicle. Similar incidents across the city have shown that too often the response comes too late, and meaningful prevention is lacking. Patrol Borough Queens North has already taken an important step by deploying a team to address these incidents.

Intro 984 would codify that approach into law, expand it citywide, establish a unit to monitor publicly available information about planned takeovers, and require the NYPD to report to the Council so we can measure its effectiveness and ensure proper oversight. But a specialized unit alone is not enough. We also need more police officers assigned to our local precincts so they have the staffing necessary to prevent these incidents, respond quickly, and maintain public safety throughout our neighborhoods. I ask my colleagues to sign onto Intro 984 so we can advance a serious, permanent, and accountable solution to this growing public safety threat. Thank you.
Council Member Thomas-Henry, followed by Council Member Sanchez, and Council Member Santosuosso, we’ll come back to her when she’s ready.

Thank you, Majority Leader.

There's a saying we've all heard: if you can make it in New York, you can make it anywhere. New Yorkers have always understood that this city comes with a price. We accept that. I mean, the New York mindset is often anchored on blind faith that success is just on the other side of grinding harder. But there's a thin line between paying a premium to live in New York and being priced out of New York. Every additional increase moves more families and more small businesses closer to that line. I believe good government meets people where they are, and right now, New Yorkers are telling us exactly where they are. They're making impossible choices between paying bills and putting food on the table. As Chair of the Committee on Small Business, I hear this every single day. For a small business owner, utilities are the only way doors stay open. They aren't a luxury. They're the operating systems of our communities — the refrigerator keeping food fresh, the salon chair staying occupied, the neighborhood laundromat running

another load, the corner bodega keeping its shelves stocked. That's why I'm proud to introduce Resolution 561, calling on our utility companies and the Public Service Commission to freeze utility rates for New York City residents. Families are juggling housing, groceries, childcare, and transportation. Seniors living on fixed incomes have the least room for yet another increase. Our small businesses are navigating higher rents, rising insurance costs, and inflation. Utility bills shouldn't be the breaking point. An affordable city isn't built by asking people to absorb one more bill. Today we're asking for something simple: a pause, a freeze, and a recognition that affordability must remain the center of every decision. Thank you to my colleagues who have already joined me in supporting this effort. I encourage the rest of the Council to join us. I would also like to acknowledge one of my SYEP (Summer Youth Employment) interns who is in the

Chamber. Although he hails from the BX in Council Member Riley's district, he has proven to be (TIMER) an invaluable member of our team. I also want to acknowledge my nephew, who is visiting before starting his freshman year at UT Dallas. Thank you.
Council Member Pierina Sanchez, followed by Council Santosuosso, then Council Member Brewer.

Thank you, Majority Leader. I make these remarks on behalf of my community. In less than a year, serious allegations of sexual misconduct have emerged against two successive commanding officers in the NYPD's 46th Precinct, including allegations that have now led to a criminal indictment. This represents an alarming pattern of alleged abuse of power, and I call on the Mayor and the police commissioner to cooperate fully with all criminal and civil investigations, ensure a thorough and transparent internal disciplinary process, and act swiftly to restore stability, accountability, and

trust within the 46th NYPD command. In the context of our challenges, our community is outraged and deeply saddened by these allegations. Even as crime continues to decline citywide, West Bronx residents continue to endure some of the highest levels of violence in our city, including just last night, when a horrific homicide occurred outside of a lounge that I have previously brought to the NYPD 46th Precinct commander and had flagged for City Hall. At such a critical moment, our community cannot afford a leadership vacuum or instability in this precinct. I commend NYPD Commissioner Tisch for her swift move to fire the officer accused of attempted rape of a junior officer, but I also want to use this moment to call out that the public also needs to see swift action in the face of substantiated NYPD misconduct, especially in the cases of Black men and women killed by the NYPD. The hardworking people of our communities deserve more from the NYPD and from our city. We will continue to demand the highest standards of integrity

and accountability in policing alongside sustained investments in the foundations of true community safety. Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Santosuosso, followed by Council Member Brewer.

Thank you, Majority Leader. I just want to take a moment to acknowledge that on July 4th in Coney Island, there was a horrific shooting where a family was celebrating July 4th at a barbecue in a NYCHA courtyard. Eight people were shot, including two children as young as six and seven years old. Gun violence is unfortunately becoming all too common in Coney Island, despite whatever the citywide stats may say. And so I'm grateful for the 60th Precinct for apprehending the shooter. But this is a problem that we need to solve. And so I don't pretend to be an expert in this. I will be convening as many people as I can and experts on this issue to try to attack this and really solve it once and for

all. And so this is a call to action for anybody who wants to see gun violence end in our city, but also in Coney Island. Please get in touch with my office. We want to work to collectively end this problem. And my heart goes out to the family that's recovering at this time. Thank you so much.
Thank you, Council Member. Council Member Brewer, followed by Council Member Cabán.

Thank you. I do want to thank Council Member Louis for the SCRIE/DRIE, and it's going to make a huge difference for a lot of older adults. Thank you. I look forward to working with you. So I love interns. I want to thank those who are here today. I respect them, and it's a pleasure to work with you: Phoebe Adler, second year at Middlebury College; Evangelita Benassi, McGill University; Xavier Brenner, who's a second year at Barnard College; Rebecca Chen, who's also second year

at Barnard College, and she's a food influencer; Asha Gorodnik, sophomore at Trinity School; Matteo Gregorio, senior at Oberlin College; Isaac Ho, University of Buffalo; Julia Hornich, who is at Macaulay Honors College; third year, James Lu, who is a Van Fellow and also will be getting a second or maybe third degree, the National Chengchi University in Taiwan; Sienna Link Morris, who's third year at NYU Tisch; Adam Moss, who's a sophomore at Stuyvesant High School; Ella Williams at Horace Mann School; and Veronica Hunt, who's a junior at Trinity School Thank you all. That's just a few of the interns we have in our office. I thank each and every one of you. Thank you.

All right, Council Member Cabán, followed Council Member Morano. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. I want to echo the sentiments of Council Member Sanchez. It is great to see that the commissioner is willing to swiftly fire an officer who commits an act of abuse of power and violence against a coworker. I would like to see the same

swiftness when there are substantiated claims of not just violence against Black and brown New Yorkers, but the killings, the murders of Black and brown New Yorkers who not only continue to stay on the force, but continue to get raises, to get promoted, to get their pensions. And it says a lot to say where the action is happening, and where it isn't. With that, I want to shift gears and take a moment to just acknowledge a New Yorker who has just dedicated so much of himself, his time, his energy to a progressive vision, towards a progressive vision that delivers safety and justice and affordability for working people across our city. the Progressive Caucus. Can't wait to see what you do next with Council Member Hanif.

Thank you, Majority Leader. Today, I'm introducing Resolution 555 that speaks to something everyone of us has heard about from our constituents, irrespective of party or borough: utility bills that just keep going up. For millions of New Yorkers, electricity and natural gas aren't luxuries; they're necessities. You can postpone buying a new television set, but you can't postpone keeping the lights on, refrigerating your food, or heating your home in the winter. And yet too many New Yorkers open their utility bill every month and ask the same question: How did it get this high? This resolution doesn't pretend that the City Council controls utility rates. We don't, obviously. That's the responsibility of Albany and the Public Service Commission. But when New Yorkers

are struggling, I think it's our responsibility to speak up. And the package of state legislation that this resolution supports would provide better notice before rate hikes, require regulators to consider the impact that utility rates have on families, strengthen consumer protections, improve payment plan standards, and bring greater transparency and accountability to utility regulations. These are not radical ideas at all. They are common-sense, nonpartisan reforms rooted in good government. Whether you're a homeowner on Staten Island, a tenant in the Bronx, or a small business owner in Brooklyn, everyone deserves to know what they're paying for, why costs are increasing, and whether someone is truly looking out for the people paying the bills, not just the entities that are sending them. This shouldn't be a Republican or Democratic issue. It's a kitchen table issue. Every dollar a family spends unnecessarily on utility bills is a dollar they can't spend on groceries, rent, prescriptions, or saving for their children's future.

Government can't solve every problem overnight, but we can insist on greater transparency. We can demand accountability, and we can stand with the people who work hard, pay their bills, and simply want a fair deal. So I hope my colleagues will join me in supporting this resolution and sending a clear message to Albany. New Yorkers deserve an energy system that's not only reliable but affordable, transparent, and worthy of the public's trust. Thank you. (TIMER)
Council Member Riley, followed by Council Member Avilés.

Thank you, Majority Leader. Today, I'm proud to introduce Intro 981, legislation that takes an important first step toward exploring how New York City can expand access to responsible, community-focused financial investments. This bill establishes a task force to study the feasibility of creating a municipal public bank and to develop recommendations for what such an

institution could look like here in New York City. Bringing together experts in community banking, small businesses, labor, economic development, and consumer advocacy will ensure this conversation is informed by a broad range of perspectives and grounded in the needs of the communities we serve. The task force will evaluate governance, capitalization, financial management, regulatory compliance, and long term sustainability before issuing a comprehensive report with recommendations to guide future policymaking. By requiring a transparent, data-driven process, this legislation ensures that any future decisions are based on thoughtful analysis, stakeholder engagement, and sound financial planning. As our city continues to explore new ways to strengthen local economies, support small businesses, and expand access to capital, we have a responsibility to carefully examine every viable option.

This legislation does exactly that. It creates a framework for informed decision-making while prioritizing accountability, transparency, and the long term interests of New Yorkers. I want to thank Council Members Joseph, Cabán, Stevens, Epstein, and Avilés for co-priming this bill, and I look forward to working with the rest of my colleagues and stakeholders as this conversation continues. Thank you, Majority Leader. Today, I'm introducing a resolution calling for reform of the New York City public school governance. Resolution 548 calls on the State Legislature to amend our city's education law to grant the City Council representation on the Panel for Educational Policy, and to give Community

Education Councils more oversight over DOE hiring decisions. The PEP wields immense power in our city. They oversee school closures, co-locations, grade reconfigurations, and massive DOE contracts, including those exceeding $1 million. Their actions affect nearly one million students and 140,000 DOE staff members. And yet, of the PEP's voting members, none are selected by the City Council. The City Council, which oversees and adopts the budget that funds the DOE, does not have any representation on the PEP. Giving the City Council a seat would help democratize the panel and ensure that our communities are adequately represented in decisions that affect them. Community Education Councils face a similar imbalance. While CECs help identify candidates for superintendent and submit evaluations, they have no meaningful authority over leadership decisions within their district. The State should amend the system to allow

for CECs, a body that directly represents parents within their school district, to have more of a say in decision making. Granting the Council a designated seat on the PEP and giving CECs a stronger role in hiring decisions within their districts would add a necessary measure of legislative and community accountability to the largest public school system in the United States. I’d like to thank you again, Majority Leader, for the opportunity to speak on this resolution.
